summary: Internal planning to rewrite the launch runbook after the recent traffic spike. Primary goals: ringfence high-risk paths, simplify decision tree for oncall, add automated mitigations for KV cache thrash and aggressive batching, and schedule a canary for the new routing rule. We prioritized minimal user-visible disruption and clarified handoffs between SRE, release, and product.
topics: Runbook rewrite: decision trees and automated mitigations
Docs & comms: external TL;DR and internal triage flow

Date: 2026-04-07
Start: 16:30 UTC
Duration: ~80 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Rafael Soto, Priya Nair, Ethan Moore, Zoe Patel, Ana Gomez, Samir Desai, Liam O'Connor, Harpreet Kaur

transcript:
[00:00] Maya: All right folks, thanks for joining. We're here to move the runbook out of notes and into something that oncall can actually follow after last week's traffic spike. start with a quick recap from Rafael.
[00:24] Rafael: Sure, I can do a quick one. So on April 2 we saw a traffic multiplier around 6x for a sustained 12 minutes which blew through our default batching expectations, kv cache churn went high, and several inference processes dropped to fallback kernels. We had increased tail latency, and the autoscaler bounced which added capacity but introduced transient overloads. There was some noise in the metrics pipeline itself so pagers were noisy.
[00:56] Ana (overlap): and to add — one of the things that bit us was the prefix cache invalidation pattern from a customer test which coincidentally ran at the same time, so two things aligned.
[01:12] Priya: Important callout. We should make sure the runbook separates 'external spike' from 'internal burst' so ops know to look for running experiments.
[01:26] Maya: Agreed. Rafael, can you walk through the five failure modes you captured?
[01:32] Rafael: Yeah list is: kv cache saturation, batching window overgrowth, kernel fallback thrash, autoscaler oscillation, and noisy alerts caused by metric aggregation lag. I put rough mitigation steps next to each in the doc but we need clearer steps that can be executed with minimal context.
[01:52] Ethan: On the kv cache front, we discussed an eviction-first ringfence earlier — basically if the prefix cache is over threshold we route new requests to a light path that skips the big prefix cache and uses a smaller, quantized model variant. That reduces mem pressure and gives us an exit. We prototype that in the traffic router.
[02:15] Samir: Quick clarifying question, is that the same as the kernel-variant fallback we used in March? there were some perf regressions there.
[02:24] Rafael: Related but different. Kernel-variant fallback flipped execution kernels (e.g., CPU fallback or non-optimized kernels) whereas the ringfence routing intentionally sends to smaller model variants or local cpu-only cheap model to preserve availability. We need both in the runbook and order of operations.
[02:44] Zoe: From QA's perspective, we need deterministic test cases: p95 burst, 3-minute sustained multiplier, and kludgy customer experiment. Also need smoke for SLO and data correctness.
[02:58] Harpreet: I'll draft a TL;DR that's suitable for customer comms — short, non-technical, and then an internal fuller postmortem. Want to make sure we aren't oversharing.
[03:09] Priya: Ok, in the runbook we should have three levels: observer steps, mitigation steps (automated if present), and escalation steps. Each mitigation should include a revert path and an SLA impact note.
[03:26] Liam: For release gating, we should require canary of the ringfence routing on 5% traffic, validated for 24 hours, before shipping the change to prod routing. Also add a kill-switch in the control plane enabled by the release owner.
[03:43] Maya: Good. Let's talk about automation — Rafael, which mitigations can we automate fast?
[03:50] Rafael: The easiest is alert suppression for known noisy metrics with a short debounce; second is automatic routing to a warm standby quantized model when kv eviction crosses threshold; third is a smart autoscaler cooldown tweak — but that one needs more testing.
[04:05] Ethan: Building the routing prototype won't be huge — a config flag and a simple policy in the router. The complexity is validating model compatibility and KV cache priming. I'll need a list of safe model variants.
[04:19] Maya: Priya, can you enumerate the ownership mapping in the doc? Who owns the canary, who flips the kill-switch, who owns customer comms?
[04:26] Priya: Yes — canary owner: Release Eng (Liam), kill-switch: SRE (Rafael), comms: Product (Maya + Harpreet), metrics verification: QA (Zoe). I'll put that mapping into the runbook.
[04:38] Rafael: Also add a step to capture heap snapshots and kernel histograms automatically when we detect the eviction spike — we were missing some of that last time.
[04:47] Ana: and include a list of the quick queries to run in grafana — top hosts, model variance, kv miss ratio, and autoscaler events.
[04:59] Maya: Let's try to walk through an example play — I want a concise script that an oncall can run within 5 minutes. Rafael?
[05:06] Rafael: Script: 1) check metric panel (link), 2) confirm kv miss ratio > 15% and sustained for 2 minutes, 3) flip route-to-small-model for the least critical header group, 4) monitor p95 for 5 mins, 5) if improvement, leave ringfence on and open an incident ticket; else rollback. I've put a one-liner curl for the flip in the doc.
[05:36] Zoe: QA needs the canary checklist updated — include data integrity checks for embeddings and generation length. We caught an off-by-one batch bug last time.
[05:46] Ethan: On the technical debt side, I want to capture two follow-ups: move kernel fallback to be per-host not per-cluster, and add a lightweight kv store tier for extreme prefix hits. Those are medium-term but belong in the runbook appendix.
[06:02] Samir: Any regulatory concerns with routing to quantized models? e.g., customers under private deployments — that needs opt-in or a policy check.
[06:11] Priya: Good flag. We'll gate ringfence on customer tier — dedicated/private customers should be out by default unless they opt-in. Add a check in the routing policy.
[06:21] Maya: Let's talk about communications cadence: first internal alert + short pasteboard for execs, second a public-safe line for customers if incident impacts more than 5% of requests. Harpreet will own the customer note.
[06:35] Harpreet: I'll prepare two templates: internal short bullet list and a short public note. Need approval from legal if we mention root cause.
[06:44] Maya: Competitor note — a few teams asked about how others handle this; some vendors simply take requests offline which we don't want to do. Keep that in mind when we propose fallback quality vs availability.
[06:57] Rafael: Also add a section in runbook for metric hygiene — which alerts are primary vs noise, and add a brief training for oncall to reduce cognitive load.
[07:08] Priya: On the timeline: aim for runbook draft v1 by 2026-04-09, prototype routing by 04-14, canary scheduled 04-20 to 04-22 window, and post-canary retro 04-24.
[07:22] Maya: Anything else?
[07:25] Liam: Just one ask — make the kill-switch accessible from both the release console and a simple curl endpoint. We had the console locked down during the spike and it slowed us.
[07:36] Ethan: I'll add the endpoint and short auth doc.
[07:39] Zoe: I'll bake the test scenarios into the canary plan and create automated runbooks for them.
[07:44] Harpreet: I'll post the public TL;DR as a draft in the doc and ping legal.
[07:49] Maya: Great. Quick recap — Rafael to enumerate failure modes into crisp steps, Ethan to prototype ringfence routing, Harpreet to draft comms, Priya to own mapping and checklist updates, Zoe to update QA canary tests. We reconvene 2026-04-13 for a pre-canary dry run. Any objections?
[08:06] Ana: No objections.
[08:08] Samir: none.
[08:10] Maya: Ok call ends. Links and action items in the doc.

Note: Transcript contains natural speech artifacts, occasional crosstalk, and imperfect transcription of some technical terms (e.g., kv vs K-V, kernel fallback named as 'kernel-flap' in one place).
